theme: The great high priest; warning and assurance
readingInstruction: Read Hebrews 4:14-6:20. The reading has three movements: the invitation to draw near to a sympathetic high priest, the qualifications of a priest, and a sober warning followed by a promise. Slow down at 6:4-8 and 6:9-12. The warning is real, and so is the author’s confidence that his readers will persevere.
settingTheScene: The author has spoken of Jesus as a great high priest. Now he stops to explain what that means. A priest stands between God and humanity, offering gifts and sacrifices on behalf of the people. In Israel the priests came from the tribe of Levi and the high priest from the line of Aaron. How could Jesus be a priest when he came from Judah? The author’s answer introduces a mysterious figure from Genesis 14 and Psalm 110: Melchizedek. But before he can fully explain, he pauses to rebuke his readers for being slow to understand and to warn them against falling away. Then he ends the chapter with one of the most encouraging passages in the New Testament, on the certainty of God’s promise.
observation: 4:14-16 repeats the call to hold fast and gives the invitation to draw near to the throne of grace.
A high priest is chosen from among men to act on their behalf, and he can deal gently with the ignorant because he is beset by weakness himself (5:1-3).
Christ did not exalt himself to be a high priest. The Father called him with the words of Psalm 2 and Psalm 110 (5:5-6).
“In the days of his flesh,” Jesus offered up prayers with loud cries and tears, and “he learned obedience through what he suffered” (5:7-8).
The readers are called “dull of hearing” and still needing milk when they should be teachers (5:11-14).
6:1-2 lists elementary teachings: repentance, faith, baptisms, laying on of hands, resurrection, and judgment.
6:4-6 describes those who have been enlightened and tasted the heavenly gift, and then fallen away.
God swore by himself so that by two unchangeable things we might have strong encouragement, an anchor of the soul (6:13-20).
interpretation:
The passage opens by repeating the invitation. The repetition is deliberate. Having just warned his readers, the author immediately offers hope. We have a high priest. Come to the throne of grace. Between the warning and the hope, he wants them to see that the answer to weakness is not retreat but nearness.

Chapter 5 sets out what a priest is and shows that Jesus qualifies. The two qualifications are sympathy and appointment. A high priest must be able to deal gently with those who stray because he knows his own weakness. Jesus meets this qualification not through sin but through suffering. “In the days of his flesh” refers to his earthly life, and verse 7 almost certainly points to Gethsemane. The Son offered prayers with loud cries and tears. This is the picture of a Savior who knows what it is to pray in agony. He “learned obedience through what he suffered.” This does not mean he was ever disobedient, but that he experienced obedience at its hardest cost. Having been “made perfect,” he became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey him. The second qualification is appointment: Jesus did not claim the office for himself. The Father called him, and Psalm 110:4 identifies his priesthood as “after the order of Melchizedek.”

At this point, the author’s thought stalls. He has much to say about Melchizedek, but his readers are sluggish. They should be teachers, yet they need to be taught the basics again. The rebuke is pastoral rather than cruel, and it is a challenge to every Christian: are you growing? Solid food belongs to the mature, those who have trained themselves by practice to distinguish good from evil.

Then comes the warning in 6:4-8. It is one of the most debated passages in the Bible, and honest interpreters disagree. The best reading, in line with the whole letter, is that the author describes those who have shared in the visible blessings of the church community, heard the word, and tasted its power, but who then deliberately and finally reject Christ. For such a person, there is no second sacrifice. If Christ’s sacrifice is rejected, nothing else remains. The author illustrates with farmland: the same rain falls on the field that bears fruit and the field that bears thorns. The question is what the field produces.

But the author does not leave his readers terrified. “Though we speak in this way, yet in your case, beloved, we feel sure of better things.” The evidence of genuine faith is love shown through service to the saints, and the author wants them to keep it up to the end. Warnings and assurance are not enemies. The warnings are the means God uses to keep his people.

The chapter ends with a stunning image. God made a promise to Abraham and, because he had no one greater to swear by, swore by himself. A promise and an oath are two unchangeable things in which it is impossible for God to lie. This is the foundation of our confidence. Our hope is an anchor for the soul, firm and secure, and it enters “into the inner place behind the curtain” where Jesus has gone as a forerunner on our behalf. The anchor does not hold from the ship’s side but from the harbor. Our hope is anchored in heaven, in the person of Christ.
connection: The call of Jesus as priest from Psalm 110:4 links to your reading of Psalm 110 in this unit and to Genesis 14, where Abram met Melchizedek. The oath to Abraham comes from Genesis 22:16-17 and ties to the Abrahamic covenant you read in Unit 3. The picture of the field with thorns recalls Genesis 3:17-18 and Isaiah 5. Gethsemane in 5:7 anticipates Matthew 26, Mark 14, and Luke 22. The inner place behind the curtain points forward to the temple imagery of Hebrews 9-10.
application:
First, check your growth. Hebrews calls the readers to move beyond milk. What is one area of your faith, such as prayer, Scripture, or serving, in which you have stayed at the beginner level? Choose one concrete step to deepen it.

Second, treat the warning as a gift. If you feel a pull to drift or give up, do not hide it. Bring it to the Lord and to a trusted believer. The warnings exist to keep you close.

Third, rest in the oath of God. When you feel that your hold on God is slipping, remember that your hope does not rest in your grip but in his promise. The anchor holds you.

Fourth, draw near this week. Pray as someone who knows that Jesus has been where you are.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus that he is a high priest who knows what it is to weep and pray.
Ask him to keep you from sluggishness and give you hope as an anchor.
Draw near to his throne of grace and tell him what you need.
